units: a depot supervisor sets out two routes for a newly hired driver
the fast road has a recently fitted safety barrier and a toll point at its entrance
the surface of the fast road is smooth and shakes the vehicle very little
the second route runs through small towns where the surface is full of holes
traffic calming humps stand before the junctions on the second route
the driver objects that the direct run is costly and dull
the supervisor states that a broken road wears the mechanical parts more than the toll costs
the driver accepts her supervisor's view and settles on the fast route
text: The depot supervisor sat the newly hired driver down and explained that the two routes available were not equivalent. One of them, he said, follows a fast road with a freshly fitted crash barrier and a toll point at the entrance; the surface stays smooth throughout, and the vehicle barely shudders. The other winds through small towns where the tarmac is pitted with holes and where a calming hump rises before every junction on the way. She pushed back at that: the direct run costs money, and the sheer monotony of it wears a person down. He answered that a broken surface eats into the suspension considerably more than the toll ever removes from the takings, and that a single swerve into an unmarked hole costs more again. She came round in the end, and settled on the fast road.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: trade called for roadways able to carry heavy waggons
the width of the ways had to let two teams pass each other
the needs of war produced straight alignments and evenly spaced staging posts
ordinary travellers were given resting places and watering points
carved markers announced the distance still to be covered
upkeep became necessary because a neglected way decays and closes over
these old concerns are found again in the networks still being built
text: The earliest organised road networks grew out of demands that had little to do with one another. Trade came first of all: a laden waggon needed a surface firm enough not to sink under the weight it carried, and the width had to let two teams pass each other without either of them drawing to a halt. Then came the needs of war, calling for straight alignments and staging posts set at even intervals, so that a column on the move could hold together without straggling. Ordinary travellers were served later, with resting houses, watering places and carved stones telling them how far they still had left to go. Upkeep settled the matter of its own accord: a way left alone sinks, fills with thorn and turns back into a track. Those same demands shape the networks still being laid today.

units: markings on the ground show where the doors will open
you have to wait for passengers to get off before boarding
two streams meeting at the doorway slow the whole exchange
once aboard it is better to move towards the middle of the carriage
the boarding step turns slippery in rain and causes falls
it is advisable to get ready to leave one stop before the intended one
forcing the door is unwise and you can come back on the opposite line
text: Arriving on the platform, your first instinct should be locating the markings painted underfoot, which show precisely where the doors will open. Then you let people off. It sounds obvious, but two streams meeting head on clog the doorway and cost the whole carriage a good minute. Once aboard, work your way along towards the middle of the carriage instead of camping beside the entrance. The step deserves attention whenever it rains: the surface turns soapy underfoot, and a fall happens more quickly than you would imagine. Getting off, be ready a stop early, bag closed, one hand free. And if you miss your moment, whatever happens, do not force the door. Leave at the following stop, cross over, and return on the opposite line. Nothing disastrous, unless you insist on rushing to mend your mistake.

units: a front tyre tore open on the lip of a hole in the road surface
the steering snatched sharply and the coach left its line
the driver gave up braking hard so as not to unbalance the lorry behind him
he let the side barrier take the rubbing of the vehicle
the passengers heard the bodywork grinding along the metal over a long stretch
the inquiry showed that the repair of the surface had been botched
the top layer had lifted away after a wet season
what the users remember is that the barrier withstood the impact
text: A burst tyre was all it took to turn an ordinary run into an emergency manoeuvre. The coach was in the nearside lane, holding a steady speed, when the front wheel tore itself open on the lip of a badly patched hole. The steering snatched, and the vehicle slewed towards the verge. Braking hard would have swung the trailer of the lorry behind into a jack knife, so the driver came off the throttle instead and let the crash barrier take the rubbing. Passengers, thrown about in their seats, heard the bodywork grinding along the metal for a long stretch before everything came to rest. The inquiry found that the surface had been patched in haste after a wet season, and that the top layer had lifted clean away from what lay beneath. What the users remember, though, is that the barrier held.

units: loading a luggage hold is a matter of method rather than strength
the bags turn up in disorder while the space available is fixed
it is advisable to sort the bags on the ground before opening the hatch
rigid containers and soft bags are put into two separate groups
the heaviest pieces go against the rear bulkhead
soft bags fill the hollows left between the cases
the luggage for the first stop is set near the opening
a well arranged load does not shift under braking
text: Loading a luggage hold asks less of your arms than of your method, and the difficulty comes down to one thing: the bags turn up in whatever order they please, while the space you have forgives nothing. So begin outside, sorting them patiently, before the hatch is even open. Rigid cases go in one heap, soft holdalls in another, and anything due to come out along the way is kept aside. Then set the heaviest pieces flat against the rear bulkhead, edge towards you; they will make a solid footing. Push the soft bags into the hollows the cases leave, much the way you would stuff a mattress with straw. Keep the space nearest the opening for whatever leaves at the first stop. A hold built like that does not shift under braking, and unloading goes off without anything tumbling out.

units: two toll collecting systems work on the same road
the barrier arrangement forces vehicles to a complete standstill
the queue stretches back at the barrier arrangement as soon as traffic thickens
the repeated pulling away raises what the lorries burn
the automatic gantry lets vehicles through without any break in speed
the throughput measured at the gantry is markedly higher than at the barriers
the end of the braking reduces the wear of the road surface
automatic reading fails when the plates are dirty
deferred collection brings about heavier administrative handling
text: Two ways of collecting tolls now run along the same road, and the readings taken at the newly opened junction lay bare the gap between them. The barrier arrangement, with its sorting lanes, brings every vehicle to a standstill; throughput hits a ceiling, the queue stretches back as soon as traffic thickens, and the repeated pulling away drives up what the lorries burn. The overhead gantry, mounted on the slip road, lets vehicles hold their speed as they go under it; the throughput measured there runs far higher, and the surface wears more slowly once the constant braking stops. Engineers do point to a weakness: the reading fails on dirty plates, and payment falls back on billing after the event, which is a good deal heavier to handle. Smoother traffic, then, is bought with paperwork.

units: the moored vessel stretches along the whole length of the quay
a row of round openings ringed in brass runs just above the water
the level given over to vehicles looks like a vast metal hall
the boarding ramps ring out as the wheels pass over them
the cabin level is known by its narrow passageways and its numbered doors
the topmost deck takes the walkers and holds benches bolted to the floor
a lowered gangway links the stern of the vessel to the quay
two thick ropes hold the vessel against the swell
text: The moored vessel occupies the entire length of the quay, and its architecture reads upwards, level by level. Low down, the dark hull barely breaks the surface, and a line of round ports runs along it, each one ringed in brass that the salt air has dulled. Above that opens the vehicle deck, a great metal cavern where the ramps ring out beneath the crossing wheels. Next comes the cabin level, recognisable by its narrow passageways and by the numbered doors following one after another. The topmost deck is given over to walkers: benches bolted down, an unbroken rail, a signal mast, a funnel as broad as a tower. Astern, a lowered gangway reaches the concrete of the quay, and two heavy ropes, drawn taut at an angle, hold everything steady against the swell beating on the breakwater.

units: the carriageways were widened in the name of keeping cars moving
the shops were moved out to the edges where parking was plentiful
that move lengthened the distances everyone has to cover
the doubling of the lanes was followed by even thicker congestion
a recent reversal narrows the carriageways and hands space back to those on foot and on cycles
the writer refuses to see a passing fashion in this reversal
the old mistake lay in taking traffic for a fixed volume
traffic in fact depends on the lanes that are offered to it
text: Before passing judgement on the state of our streets, it is worth running back through the decisions that made them. The carriageways were widened first, in the belief that keeping cars moving would serve everybody. Shops were then pushed out to the edges, where parking was plentiful, which lengthened every journey people had to make. Congestion followed, so the lanes were doubled, and congestion came back thicker than before. Lately the order has reversed: streets are being narrowed, trees planted, room handed back to those on foot and on cycles. Call it a passing fashion if you like, but it is nothing of the sort. It corrects a mistake in reasoning several generations old, which took traffic for a fixed volume rather than a demand shaped by what is offered to it. Worth remembering before the next scheme.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the driver of the evening service had not chosen this trade at the start
she worked as a mechanic in a workshop that closed
the closing of the workshop pushed her to take her lorry licence
her mechanical experience lets her feel a worn suspension at the first speed hump
she reports faults before they cut the service short
her knowledge of the chassis makes her take obstacles gently
she had the boarding step replaced because its worn edge hindered older travellers
her route logs fewer incidents than the others
the firm has given her the training of the newly hired drivers
text: The woman who drives the evening coach never once pictured herself doing this. She started out as a mechanic in a workshop; the workshop shut, and she took her lorry licence for want of anything better. That earlier trade has come to serve her well: she can feel a tired suspension at the first speed hump, and she flags the fault up long before it strands the service. Because she knows the chassis inside out, she takes the humps gently, so her passengers no longer bump against the seat in front. She also got the boarding step changed, since a worn edge made climbing aboard risky for older travellers. The upshot is that her route logs fewer incidents than the rest, and the firm now hands her the newly hired drivers to train. She laughs about it, having only ever wanted to mend engines.

units: the coach station just opened was met with dutiful praise
the boarding bays run in one line along a single corridor
no overhead signing helps the traveller find their coach
a hurried user has to walk the whole row before spotting their departure
the hall throws back the echo and makes the spoken announcements impossible to follow
boards hung above each bay would settle the question of where to stand
absorbing materials placed under the roof would improve the hearing
the number of benches ought to be doubled
the writer judges the structure a success but its use badly thought through
text: The coach station just opened deserves better than the dutiful praise that greeted it. Its main failing is plain from the door: the boarding bays run in one long line down a single corridor, with nothing hung overhead to say which is which, so anyone in a hurry walks the whole row before spotting their coach. The hall, for its part, rings hollow and swells the announcements until nobody can make out a word. All this would amount to failure if the building offered nothing to work with; yet the remedies exist, and none of them costs much. Lit boards above each bay would settle where to stand. Absorbing panels under the roof would give the voice back its edges. As for the benches, far too few, doubling them would do. The frame is sound; it is the use of it that nobody thought through.
